strings.text: The Fisherman and his Soul

A young fisherman nets a little mermaid and loves her. To go down to her he must send his soul away — and the soul goes into the world without a heart, wearing his face. Every choice is between the one he loves and the one he was.
To love her wholly he cuts away his soul — and the soul learns from the world without a heart.
after the fairy tale by Oscar Wilde
The Shadow at his Feet
The girl dancing on the pier
Stopped, and danced
Passed by, looked back once
The Witch
“You promised.”
“Again. Without him. Till dawn.”
The heart
“And what would I love her with?”
Not to look. To cut.
“Come here once a year”
In truth: by the stone, moonlight; he stands knee-deep in the water.
Be my wife
You have a human soul. Send it away — and I will love you
What use is a soul to me? I have never seen it. Never touched it. I do not know it
She laughs and beats the water with her tail.
Send it away — and come
I will come tomorrow
What is “tomorrow”?
She laughs and goes under the water. She asked it the way one asks to take off a wet shirt — not knowing what she asks.
In truth: the Priest’s white house on the hill, morning; candles, a table for an altar. The Priest is heard, not seen yet.
Father, I love a girl of the sea. My soul is in the way. How do I send it away?
The Priest rises and makes the sign — palm to the brow and to the heart.
The soul is worth more than all the gold in the world. The sea-folk are accursed. Keep away from them
The Fisherman gets up so sharply that the bench falls, and does not hear him out.
If it is worth so much — I do not need it
Begone!
The door. On the threshold, from a boy’s habit, the Fisherman makes the same sign — and, noticing, drops his hand.
In truth: the pier at noon, a feast in the village. The dancing girl and the women are heard, not seen yet.
Noon. On the pier a girl dances barefoot, the others clap. The Fisherman walks past, toward the wood.
By the well in the fir wood lives one who knows
He comes level with the dancing girl.
Stop
He stops and looks at her feet. She pulls him by the sleeve.
Dance, fisherman!
Two clumsy steps — and he laughs, for the first time in the game. His shadow on the boards dances with him.
He walks past. He looks back once.
In truth: the well in the fir wood, evening (the moon is not up yet).
The red-haired Witch sits on the rim of the well, swinging her bare feet.
What do you want? Wind? Fish? No. I know. To send your soul away
Tell me how
The price is a dance. Tonight, at full moon, here
Only a dance?
Only
She looks at him longer than she needs to.
In truth: the same well, midnight, the moon over the firs.
The Witch beats her tambourine; they dance facing each other round the well.
By the last fir stands a man in black velvet, pale, watching. The Witch pulls the Fisherman toward him.
Bow to him
Without thinking, the Fisherman makes the sign — palm to the brow and to the heart. The man in black turns away and goes into the wood.
The Witch cries out; the dance falls apart.
The Witch by the rim of the well, breathing hard.
You broke the dance. The bargain is not kept
She watches him stand there and not go.
You promised
She looks at him a long time.
I promised
In a whisper she tells him the rule — and throws a knife at his feet.
Take it. Cut. You will see for yourself what comes of a man without one
She turns away to the well.
Again. Without him. Till dawn
She stands still — then laughs, a different laugh.
They dance, the two of them, slowly, till the moon grows pale. At dawn she gives him the knife and the rule without a word, and keeps his hand on the hilt longer than she needs to.

The rule: “At moonrise stand by the water with your back to the moon. The shadow at your feet is the body of your soul. Cut it from your feet with this knife.” The knife has a handle of green snakeskin.
In truth: the pier, the next evening, moonrise; she is by the stone, up to her shoulders in the water.
The Fisherman on the pier with his back to the moon; his shadow is long, right down to the water. By the stone the Mermaid watches.
You smell of the wood
And nothing more.
The shadow rises from the boards — a man with his face; the water shows through him.
I have been with you all your life. Do not drive me away. And if you do — do not send me without a heart. The world is cruel. Give me your heart; with it I shall not be lost
His own voice, quieter. Fear — not a plea for mercy.
Not look at it. Cut.
“My heart is hers. But come here once a year — I will come out to you.”
And what would I love her with, then?
Then I shall be cruel. You chose it yourself. Once a year I will come here and call
He looks at the water. The Soul talks to the very last.
Once a year I will come and…
It breaks off in the middle of the word.
My heart is hers. But come here once a year. I will come out to you
I will come. You promised
By the stone the Mermaid goes under the water, and does not come up for a long while.
The shadow comes away; the Soul stands apart. The Fisherman drives the knife into the post of the pier and leaves his lantern on the boards.
He walks into the water, away from the pier, toward the stone. The Mermaid waits by the stone till he is far from the Soul — then laughs, takes his hand, and they go under.
On the pier the Soul picks up his lantern and looks at the water.
And the sea took him
In truth: under the water — sand, weed, light from above in pillars; the two of them sit on the sand.
Three Years
Till sunrise
Sat beside the Soul
Went to her song
One day
“I’ll go. One day.”
“No. I stay.”
Light in pillars, weed, fish. She sings; he sits on the sand.
A year went by like a single evening
In truth: the pier, a misty dawn; he stands in the shallows up to his waist.
From the shore, his own voice:
Come out
The Fisherman comes up onto the shallows, up to his waist. On the pier stands the Soul with his lantern.
You promised. Here I am
I have been in the East. There in a cave is the Mirror of Wisdom: whoever looks in it knows everything. I hid it for you. Come
Love is better than wisdom. And I am loved
By the stone the Mermaid comes up — and swims no nearer.
Do not go near her. Whoever has her in him is not ours. That is how it is with us
Then sit with me till sunrise. Only sit. For a year I have talked to myself
Sit on the edge of the pier, beside her
Go to her song
He sits on the edge of the pier beside the Soul, not touching. The Soul tells him of the road; once she laughs — warmly, with his laugh.
The song from the stone breaks off in the middle. Down below, all that day, the Mermaid sits with her back to him.
He goes down into the water, to her song.
The Soul, alone on the pier, looks at the water and puts out the lantern.
In truth: the pier, the second year, the same day; he in the shallows.
A ring on the Soul’s finger.
I have been in the South. The Ring of Riches. Come
Love is better than riches
The Soul laughs — short and angry — and goes without a goodbye.
The Soul laughs — tiredly — and goes without a goodbye.
Show me how you dance here
We do not dance. Dancing is done with feet
He gets up and dances clumsily on the sand.
Like this — the way they do on the pier
He gets up and, without a word, dances clumsily on the sand.
She laughs and beats her tail.
Then for a long time she looks at his feet — and hides her face in her hair.
In truth: the pier, dawn of the third year; he in the shallows.
On the square beyond the bridge, where you sold your fish, a girl dances at night. You were never there at night. Her feet are like little white doves. Come. One day
You want to see feet, don’t you? Hers has none
I am tired of walking alone. You will look — and come back
You stopped that time on the pier. I remember — I danced with you
You looked back that time on the pier. I remember
To walk on the earth, let me in. On the shore I will come out again
From under the water by the stone — her song. It calls him down.
Quiet. The stone is empty.
I’ll go. One day

He laughs — short, the laugh of the pier at the feast — and in three strides over the shallows he is on the boards, wet and barefoot. The Soul gives him the lantern and steps into his shadow: there is one shadow at his feet.
Close: by the stone the Mermaid sees it, and goes under. The song breaks off.
Close: by the stone the Mermaid sees it, and goes under.
He turns to the water.
I will come back
He walks to the bridge almost at a run, not looking back.
No. I stay
As you like. Your face will be useful to me
Then I will go alone. With your face
The Soul goes over the hill with the lantern; for a long while the lantern is seen on the road to the bridge.
The Town
Without Him
Wait for the dancer
“I’ll wait till tomorrow.”
“No. Back, now.”
The cup
“It was I who took it.”
Put it back quietly
His lantern over the bridge
Rose to look
Did not lift his head
The last call
“I’ll go. I’ll give the cup back.”
“No.”
The cup, at the potter’s door
“I found it by the bridge.”
In truth: the bridge to the town, evening; beyond it — the lights.
All day he has sat under the bridge by the water. From within:
She dances at night
Evening. He walks over the bridge with the lantern; beyond it, the lights — he has never seen this town at night.
Do you hear? Music
He feels chilly, though it is warm.
In truth: the square beyond the bridge — lanterns, musicians, an empty circle on the stones.
The fisherman from the bay? Three years nobody saw you
A girl dances here…
A dancer? Never seen one. Who knows who dances of an evening
While the potter talks, the Fisherman’s hand reaches by itself for the coppers on the stall. He looks at it as at a stranger’s, catches it with his other hand and puts it behind his back.
From within, a chuckle; then:
She will be here tomorrow. I swear by the moon
Sleep at my place, if you are waiting. It is cold
I’ll wait till tomorrow
The house by the bridge: by the fire the little daughter sleeps; on the shelf, a silver cup.
My wife’s. We drank from it at our wedding
Bread, the fire. He sits down on the bench and keeps his hands under him.
No. Back, now
The potter shrugs. He turns onto the bridge. From within — not a laugh: silence.
In truth: inside the potter’s house, night, the fire low.
The Fisherman sleeps on the bench by the fire. He gets up — with his eyes shut, one shadow at his feet — goes to the shelf, takes the cup, puts it in his bag and lies down again.
The girl half opens her eyes: the guest is walking with his eyes shut. She squeezes them shut. The Fisherman does not know.
In truth: the potter’s house, morning.
The cup… My wife’s. Have you seen it?
The Fisherman reaches for his bag — it is heavy. From within:
Hush
He takes out the cup.
I don’t remember how. But the hands are mine
The potter takes it and looks at it a long time.
I gave you bread. Go
The girl hides behind her father. From within, quietly:
You said: I
While the potter bends over his daughter, the Fisherman sets the cup on the shelf behind the bread.
There it is! Rolled behind the bread
He laughs and gives bread for the road. The girl looks at the guest and says nothing. From within:
You see — nobody knows. Like me
In truth: the bridge, morning; he walks back toward the sea.
You won’t wait for the evening? Quite right. There is no dancer. There never was
You are cruel
You sent me away without a heart. I learned from the world
He walks to the sea.
In truth: the middle of the bridge, night; an old beggar asleep there, a bowl of coppers at his feet.

The Fisherman’s hand reaches by itself for the bowl; he catches it with the other and stands so, holding himself, till the trembling passes. The bowl rocks, a copper falls into the river; the old man does not wake.
You did not give me my day. And she does dance, you know. You never looked
In truth: under the water, the third year.
She sings; he listens.
They sit in silence, her hand in his.
And the Soul went over the earth alone
From above, through the water, comes a warm light — his lantern, far off, going over the bridge to the town.
Rise
He comes up to his shoulders by the stone and watches the little light go away beyond the bridge. From below the Mermaid pulls him by the hand — silently — and that evening she sings no more.
The light goes away. He does not lift his head; she lays her palm over his eyes and sings on.
In truth: the bridge and the potter’s house, evening. Here “the Fisherman” is the Soul with his face and his lantern: so people see her.
The fisherman from the bay? Three years nobody saw you. Sleep at my place; it is cold
Night. The Soul goes straight to the shelf, takes the cup, and leaves the door wide open.
Night. The Soul stands over the sleeping girl — a long time — then takes the cup.
The potter wakes; in the lantern’s light he sees the face.
Fisherman!..
The Soul goes off into the dark. Morning, the market: “The fisherman from the bay is a thief.”
By morning the whole market knows: the fisherman from the bay is a thief.
In truth: the pier, the fourth year; he in the shallows. In the Soul’s hands — the potter’s cup.
Your hands did it. I have no others
He comes up onto the shallows.
Take it back
Give it back? I don’t know how. Give it back with your own hands — or not at all
I call for the last time. Next year I shall forget the way
From below, her song calls.
Silence.
I’ll go. I’ll give the cup back
He looks a long time at the knife in the post. The Soul gives him the lantern and the cup and goes into his shadow.
By the stone the Mermaid sees it, and goes under.
He speaks to the water:
I’ll give it back — and come back
No
He turns away from the pier.
He lets go of the post and goes under the water.
In truth: the door of the potter’s house, a day’s walk there; the Soul is in him.
The potter opens the door.
You!..
His daughter behind him. The Fisherman holds out the cup.
It was I who took it
The potter takes it.
Came himself… A thief — and came
He does not shut the door at once.
I found it by the bridge
The potter takes it. He saw the face that night.
Found it, then
The door shuts.
There. Now back to your fish
The Shore
A night at sea
Went out for the night
Stayed by the water
The wave
Stayed with her
Drew her away from the water
In truth: the pier, evening; back from the town.
In truth: the pier, night; back from the town.
In truth: the pier, a misty morning; back from the town.
He hangs the lantern on the post and calls.
You swore by the sea to come whenever I call. I am calling!
And the oath answers: from the deep, the four notes of her song — they break off on the third.
You always came by yourself… Come
He has nothing to call her by. From the deep — the same four notes.
He has nothing to call her by. Only the water.
Only you can see it: far off by the stone, under the water, a pale light. It stays there. It does not rise.
Come out. You promised to come out on the shore
I promised. I lied
He pulls the knife out of the post — it is rusty.
I’ll cut you off again
The same gesture as at moonrise — and the knife goes through the shadow as through water.
A knife cuts once. You cut me off yourself
He drives the knife back into the post.
In truth: the shore by the pier — a hut of willow rods; autumn, then snow on the boards.
He weaves a hut of rods by the water. Autumn; snow on the pier; every evening he calls.
Along the frozen shore comes the Witch.
She stops.
I told you: you will see for yourself
She laughs and goes.
She puts bread and her shawl down by the hut.
The night is long. It is warm by the well
She goes, looking back.
Go to her. She is warm. She has feet
The Fisherman does not get up.
The Fisherman does not get up. The shawl lies there by the door of the hut.
In truth: the shore in spring; a widow with two children by her husband’s boat, drawn up on the sand. She is heard, not seen yet.
A widow with two children, by the boat of her husband who did not come back in the storm. She asks for nothing.
There are no fish. When the ice goes, we’ll leave. Somewhere
Before she says more, she looks at him a long time, and puts the children behind her.
The boat is rotting. Take it, if you need it
The children look at the net on the rail. From within:
You are the best fisherman in the bay. Go out for one night — for them. What harm is there?
Go out for the night
Stay
The widow’s boat, his lantern on the bow, his net.
The net is full.
The widow nods. In the morning she takes the children over the bridge with their bundles, who knows where; the younger looks back at the net on the rail. At night he is alone on the pier.
In truth: the widow’s boat at sea, night.
In truth: the pier, night.
Under the keel passes a pale light, and for a moment — four notes. He thinks he is dreaming, and draws in the net.
I tempted you with evil and with good. Let me at least into your heart — to be one, as before
Come in
I cannot. It is all taken up with her
In truth: the shore by the pier, dawn.
In truth: the shore by the pier, night.
Dawn. He comes in with a full net and hangs the lantern on the post. The widow sees the fish.
If the boat goes out — we’ll stay
On the sand the widow’s children stand over something, and step apart. It is the Mermaid. Dead.
Night. A black wave lays the Mermaid at his feet. Dead.
He is on his knees; he kisses the cold lips.
I loved you more than wisdom. More than riches. You called — and I did not hear
The sea grows dark and comes toward the shore.
Without turning round, to the children:
Home! Run!
They run up the shore.
Run! The sea is coming!
The sea cast you out…
In truth: the shore; she lies on the sand at his knees, the wave coming.
Stay with her
Draw her away from the water
Her hand in his while the wave comes. His heart breaks — and the Soul goes into his heart.
He wraps her in his net and draws her up the shore, backing away.
The wave strikes the hut and carries it off. Up at the edge of the field where the linen is bleached he falls beside her. His heart breaks — and the Soul goes into his heart.
The Soul goes in without a word, and he shudders with cold.
I am home
The wave covers them.
Epilogue
In truth: the shore by the pier, morning; the two of them on the sand, he holding her.
White Flowers
Morning. The lantern still burns on the post. The Priest comes down to bless the sea; on the sand lie two — the Fisherman holding her in his arms.
I will not bless the sea. Accursed are the sea-folk, and accursed are they who go with them
He sold his soul — and turned thief
He pulls the knife out of the post and throws it into the sea.
Bury them in the corner of the field where the linen is bleached. With no sign
In truth: the edge of the field where the linen is bleached, morning; a fresh mound.
A Lantern on the Pier
Morning. At the edge of the field — a fresh mound. The Fisherman goes down to the pier — the post has stood — pulls out the knife and sets it at her head. He sits beside her.
Who is here?
She is from the sea
And a thief, they say
The Fisherman does not answer.
She shall not lie in holy ground. And you — come away from her. Begone!
The Fisherman does not get up. The Priest goes, without a blessing.
In truth: the pier, the same morning as the last call.
Two Lights
The Soul leaves the pier with the cup and the lantern. The lantern is dark; she does not turn round. Over the hill, to the bridge.
The Soul leaves the pier with the cup and the lantern. The lantern burns; once she turns to the water. Over the hill, to the bridge.
In truth: the Priest’s house on the hill, years later; the crowd at the door, the Witch among them.
The fisherman from the bay sold his soul — and see, now he thieves from town to town
The women make the sign.
The Witch in the crowd laughs aloud.
Sold! He gave it away for nothing — I saw
And afterwards she pulls the knife out of the post and carries it away.
And at full moon she dances alone at the end of the pier.
In truth: the Priest’s white house, three years later, a feast day.
Three years. On the altar — white flowers such as no one has seen, and their scent. The Priest meant to speak of wrath — and speaks of love, not knowing why himself.
Where are the flowers from?
From the corner of the field where the linen is bleached.
To that corner the widow’s children carry shells: they stayed, the boat goes out again.
To that corner nobody goes.
In the morning the Priest goes down to the sea and blesses everything — the water, the fish, the sea-folk. But the sea-folk had left the bay, and there were never flowers in that corner again.
In truth: the pier in the mist; the Priest on it, the empty hook of the lantern.
Last shot: the Priest on the pier in the mist, the lantern’s hook empty. Far off, at the edge of hearing, four notes, going away out of the bay.
Last shot: the Priest on the pier in the mist, the lantern’s hook empty. Only the water.
In truth: the Priest’s door, three springs later.
Three springs. On the mound — white flowers such as no one has seen. The Fisherman carries them to the Priest’s door, lays them on the threshold and goes.
The Priest sets them on the altar; he meant to speak of wrath — and speaks of love. The next day he blesses the sea. The sea-folk have left the bay.
In truth: the pier at night, many years later; the Fisherman is old.
Last shot: night; the old Fisherman at the end of the pier with his lantern, its beam on the water. Beside him the widow’s boy knots a new net from his. He hears no notes — only the water.
Last shot: night; the old Fisherman alone at the end of the pier with his lantern, its beam on the water. Sometimes he seems to hear three notes.
Last shot: night; the old Fisherman alone at the end of the pier with his lantern, its beam on the water. Only the water.
In truth: under the water by the stone, years on. His hair is white; she is the same as in the net.
She touches his hair.
What is this — white?
Years
What are “years”?
He does not answer.
He is the first to take her hand, as he always called her.
She takes his hand first, before he reaches for hers.
She sings all four notes.
She begins to sing and falls silent; they are silent, hand in hand.
Last shot: night, the bay; under the water by the stone, two pale lights; far off beyond the hill, a third, going away.
The Net
The net
For her word
For nothing
In truth: the boat by the stone in the bay, at night; the lantern on her bow.
Every evening the young Fisherman went out upon the sea, and threw his nets into the water
The moon’s path on the water, the boat by the stone, a lantern on the bow. The Fisherman draws in his net — it is heavy, the boat heels.
Either all the fish of the sea — or trouble
In the net, asleep, lies a little Mermaid: her hair is like wet gold, her tail is silver. She opens her eyes — and struggles.
Let me go! I am the only daughter of an old father. He is alone
He holds the edge of the net so that the thread does not cut her arm, and looks at her, and cannot look away.
In truth: the boat by the stone; she is in his net.
“I will let you go if you come whenever I call, and sing to me.”
“Swim.”
I will let you go if you come whenever I call, and sing to me
She looks up at him from the net.
I will come. I swear it by the sea
She goes under the water and does not look back.
Swim
She lingers by the side of the boat.
Do you want nothing?
He says nothing. She goes — and turns once to look at him.
In truth: the stone in the bay, evening after evening.
The evenings go by one after another. Every evening he calls — and she is on the stone; every evening she sings, and the fish come into his net. She sings looking at the fish.
The first nights — an empty sea; he sits in the boat till dawn.
Then she is on the stone by herself, before any call, and sings looking at him. And then again an evening when the stone is empty and the net is empty: he does not call, he only waits.
Mornings: the market on the square beyond the bridge, an hour’s walk. The potter takes his fish; the Fisherman does not count the money, and by noon he is already walking back to the water.
And he had more fish than all the fishermen of the bay; but he looked only at the stone

The heavy net drawn up hand over hand, slowly; the boat heels. Pulled too hard — the net tears at the edge, and the hole is seen on the rail of the pier all through the game. Either all the fish of the sea, or trouble.
A heavy net, and the boat heeling.
Letting Her Go
A finger held on the knot of the net — and lifted when she grows still. Not let go — the knot slides by itself and she slips out without looking at him. Letting go.
A knot of the net, and a small hand in it.
The Dance
Taps to the Witch’s tambourine, round the well, facing her. Out of step — he stumbles, and she pulls him by the hands harder and laughs. Someone else’s dance.
A tambourine, the full moon, and two dancing round the well.
The Knife
The knife drawn along the shadow at his feet, heel to toe. An uneven cut — the Soul’s left hand stays blurred, like smoke, to the end of the game. Cutting away a part of himself.
A long shadow on the boards, and a knife with a green snakeskin handle.
The Song
Ten seconds of touching nothing while she sings. Touched — she stops, laughs and begins again, nearer; after two touches she sings holding his hand. Listening, not taking.
Four notes under the water.
The Cup
The silver cup set back on the shelf behind the bread, without a sound. It rings — the potter turns, sees it on the shelf, looks at his guest a long time and gives no bread. Carrying quietly.
A silver cup, a shelf, and the potter’s back.
The Post

A finger held on the post of the pier — and let go: he goes under the water. Not let go — the fingers slip by themselves, and he goes under without looking back at the pier. The pair of the prologue’s knot: letting go of the shore.
The post of the pier, and the water below.
The Knife, Again

The same gesture as at moonrise, with the rusty knife — and the knife goes through the shadow as through water, even when the line is true. Not tried — he throws the knife on the boards, then drives it back into the post. A knife cuts once.
A rusty knife, and a shadow that is one again.
The Net, for the Children
The net drawn up from the widow’s boat, slowly. Pulled too hard — half a net; the children get fish all the same. Deciding for others.
Holding Her
Her hand held in his while the wave comes, ten seconds. It slips — he stays beside her, their fingers almost touching (it shows in the epilogue). Not letting go.
Her cold hand, and the black wave coming.
The Net, Up the Shore

Her body wrapped in his net, drawn up the shore, backing away, slowly. Too hard — the wave reaches his knees, the net tears wider; he draws her out all the same. The same net that drew her out in the prologue.
A net with her in it, the shore, and the sea behind.

Soul
Mermaid

Priest
Potter
Widow
Girl
Women
The Soul
The Soul grows harder
The Soul longs
The Soul — how much the world without a heart has taught her. 0–2: she longs for him; 3–4: she has grown hard.
Her song
Her song sounds
Her song grows quiet
Her song — the song she sings to him. 2–3: it sounds; 0–1: it has fallen silent.
She swore by the sea to come whenever you call.
You let her go for nothing: she will come when she wants.
You danced on the pier.
The Witch will remember: you held her to her word.
The Witch will remember: you danced with her till dawn.
You promised the Soul: once a year you will come out to her.
By evening the whole market knows: the fisherman from the bay is a thief.
You went out for the widow’s children.
You stayed by the water. The widow’s children went away.
Next
A mini-game to be: for now, press the mark.
